_about: Spectral features SPHEREx can see (0.75-5.0 um, resolving power ~35-130, so only broad bands). Each band: lo/hi in um, type absorption = dip, emission = bump. side_um = width of continuum windows used either side when measuring depth. Refs are journal citations; check ADS before quoting on a slide.

brown_dwarf.label: Brown dwarf
brown_dwarf.plain: Too small to burn hydrogen. Cool enough that water and methane form in its air and carve deep dips. Most light leaks out near 4-5 um.

bands.plain: Methane - only in T and Y dwarfs, cooler than ~1300 K
Clear window: far brighter here than a normal star would be, because light from deep hot layers escapes
Carbon monoxide stirred up from deep layers

m_dwarf.label: Red dwarf star
m_dwarf.plain: Small cool star. Smooth curve falling toward long wavelengths, with mild water and CO dips.

bands.plain: Weak water - only cool stars show it

mira.label: Mira variable (pulsating red giant)
mira.plain: Huge cool giant that swells and shrinks over ~250 days. Thick water layers around it make very deep dips; brightness changes a lot between epochs.

young_star.label: Young star with a disk
young_star.plain: Star still forming planets. A warm dust disk adds extra infrared light, so the curve stays high past 2 um instead of falling.

bands.plain: Infrared excess from warm disk dust
Hot hydrogen gas falling onto the star - may be too narrow for SPHEREx

comet.label: Comet
comet.plain: Ice ball warming near the Sun. Sunlight reflects off dust, and gases glow at their own wavelengths.

bands.plain: Organic molecules such as methanol and ethane
Carbon dioxide gas - blocked by Earth's air, only seen from space

asteroid.label: Asteroid
asteroid.plain: Rock reflecting sunlight. Minerals dent the curve near 1 and 2 um; past ~3.5 um its own warmth adds light.
